summary.summary: St Helens ran a deliberately under-borrowed book in 2025/26, funding capital spend from its own cash while taking one £25m PWLB loan in April 2025 at 4.59% to lock in a rate — and the report warns more borrowing 'will be required imminently' for capital schemes. Debt stood at £157.5m at 31 March 2026 against a £220.7m borrowing need, with investments of £97.2m (including £15.1m held for Merseyside Recycling and Waste Authority and £10.3m for schools). Net treasury costs came in £2.8m under budget at £1.8m, helped by deferred borrowing and above-benchmark investment returns. £15m of LOBO loans are profiled at their next lender call dates, which makes the maturity ladder look short-term even though contractual maturities exceed 50 years.

signals.headline: £15m of LOBO loans profiled at their next lender call dates (treated as near-term maturities at 31 March 2026; contractual maturities are over 50 years)
signals.why: At each call date the lender can propose a higher rate, forcing the council to accept it or repay £15m at short notice.

signals.headline: £25m new PWLB loan taken April 2025 at 4.59%, with further borrowing flagged as required 'imminently' for capital schemes funded through borrowing
signals.why: A long-deferred external borrowing programme is now starting, converting internal borrowing into real market demand.

news_drafts.headline: St Helens forecasts £5.6m budget overspend early in financial year
news_drafts.lead: St Helens Council is forecasting a £5.6 million overspend for 2026/27 despite being only one month into the financial year, with the entire shortfall concentrated in children's services. The overspend is driven by continuing pressures in placements for looked-after children and demand for special educational needs support affecting both home-to-school transport and school funding. The council is offsetting this with £2 million in corporate savings described as one-off in nature, from deferring borrowing and getting higher returns on its cash investments. The overspend represents 2.3 per cent of the council's net budget of £242.7 million. The council also said failure to deliver agreed budget savings continues to present a risk.

news_drafts.headline: St Helens Council forecasts £5.6m budget overspend driven by children's services
news_drafts.lead: St Helens Council is forecasting it will spend £5.6m more than its £242.7m annual budget after just one month into the financial year. Children and Young People services alone are £7.6m over budget, with the main pressures coming from rising costs of placements for children in care and growing demand for special educational needs support in school transport and the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools. The council is offsetting part of this with £2m of temporary savings from treasury management (how the council borrows and invests spare cash), but has warned these are one-off and will not recur.

news_drafts.headline: St Helens forecasts £5.6m net overspend one month in, driven by £7.6m children's services pressure partially offset by corporate underspends
news_drafts.lead: St Helens Council is forecasting a net budget overspend of £5.6 million for the financial year, only one month in, concentrated almost entirely in children's services. The entire portfolio overspend of £7.6 million is driven by rising costs of placements for children looked after and demand pressures in support for children with special educational needs and disabilities, the council's budget report shows. The pressure is being offset only by one-off corporate underspends of £2 million from treasury management and deferred borrowing, which the council acknowledges will not recur. The overspend emerges as the council continues to struggle with delivering agreed budget savings, which the papers identify as "a continuing key risk." Adult social care is balanced, though the council notes further work will be needed during the year as demand grows.

findings.committee: Children and Young People Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: SEND Home to School Transport Addressing the Budget Overspend - Scrutiny Committee Report September 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: Policy reform for 16–18 and 19–25 age groups is under development with Cabinet decision scheduled for November 2026
findings.detail: The council is designing policy changes for post-16 and post-19 provision options to be presented to Cabinet. An Equality Impact Assessment is being completed to assess impact on disabled young people and lower-income families, with mitigations including needs assessment, personal travel budgets, and appeal routes.
findings.matters: Policy reform is a key lever for the savings plan, but the EIA signals potential for legal or reputational challenge; contested changes could delay or reduce the savings forecast.
findings.quote: 16–18 Provision: Two options will be presented for decision at Cabinet (November 2026); 19–25 Provision: Options will be presented for decision at Cabinet (November 2026)

findings.committee: Children and Young People Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: SEND Home to School Transport Addressing the Budget Overspend - Scrutiny Committee Report September 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: St Helens carries above-average SEND demand due to higher deprivation and free school meal eligibility, both factors associated with higher SEND prevalence
findings.detail: The paper identifies that St Helens' deprivation profile and higher proportion of pupils eligible for free school meals correlate with higher SEND prevalence and greater reliance on funded transport. This means the council's cost base is lifted by demographics beyond its control.
findings.matters: Explains why St Helens' SEND transport costs may structurally exceed comparable councils; relevant to understanding sustainability and funding discussions.
findings.figures: higher-than-average deprivation; higher proportion of pupils eligible for free school meals
findings.quote: St Helens also has a higher-than-average level of deprivation and a higher proportion of pupils eligible for free school meals, both of which correlate with higher SEND prevalence and greater reliance on the service.

findings.committee: Children and Young People Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: SEND Home to School Transport Addressing the Budget Overspend - Scrutiny Committee Report September 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: 52 pupils travel via single-occupancy routes at approximately £20,000 per pupil per annum
findings.detail: The paper identifies solo (single-occupancy) transport as a high-cost operational model and a specific target for reform. This subset alone represents over £1m of transport spend per annum and is flagged for policy change, suggesting this is seen as a key lever for cost reduction.
findings.matters: Shows a specific operational inefficiency that is quantified and targeted; indicates potential for cost reduction if the proposed policy changes land, but also a flashpoint given that consolidation may affect individual placement quality.
findings.figures: 52 pupils; approximately £20,000 per pupil per annum
findings.quote: As an example, 52 pupils currently travel via single-occupancy routes at an average cost of approximately £20,000 per pupil per annum.

findings.committee: Children and Young People Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: SEND Home to School Transport Addressing the Budget Overspend - Scrutiny Committee Report September 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: Transformation programme claims up to £2.4m savings over three years but has not yet quantified the financial benefit with sufficient certainty
findings.detail: The council's Phase 2 response (April 2026 – March 2027) aims to deliver stated savings, but section 8.2 explicitly states: 'further detailed financial modelling is required' and 'it is not possible to quantify with sufficient certainty the level of recurring savings or cost avoidance that may be achieved.' Financial modelling is to continue alongside policy development.
findings.matters: The council is reporting a plan to close a £1.7m annual deficit but the financial case has not yet been built; this is a risk to delivery and to budget forecast accuracy.
findings.figures: up to £2.4m over three years (savings target); £1.72m forecast annual overspend (gap to close)
findings.quote: further detailed financial modelling is required to assess the extent and timing of any financial benefits arising from the proposed interventions. At this stage, it is not possible to quantify with sufficient certainty the level of recurring savings or cost avoidance that may be achieved.

findings.committee: Children and Young People Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: SEND Home to School Transport Addressing the Budget Overspend - Scrutiny Committee Report September 2026 FINAL
findings.headline: Demand growth is structural: SEND cohort has grown 363% since 2014 reforms, with only 3 in-borough specialist schools forcing costly out-of-borough placements
findings.detail: The paper identifies two linked structural drivers: the education reforms changed SEND identification, expanding the cohort dramatically; simultaneously, St Helens lacks capacity in specialist school provision, forcing the majority of pupils into out-of-borough placements at higher transport cost. This is not a transient problem.
findings.matters: Shows the overspend is demand-driven and likely persistent; absence of in-borough supply means the council cannot solve it unilaterally through efficiency alone.
findings.figures: 363% increase in SEND cohort since 2014 reforms; only 3 specialist schools in St Helens
findings.quote: Growth in the SEND cohort: the number of children defined as SEND has risen by 363% since the 2014 SEND reforms, directly increasing statutory transport demand. Limited in-borough specialist provision: with only three specialist schools in St Helens, a high proportion of children are placed out of borough, generating longer and more expensive journeys.

daily_post.headline: The council faces a £6.8m forecast budget gap in 2028/29, with core spending power increases well below the national average.
daily_post.lead: The council is receiving below-average funding while demand pressures mount; the 2028/29 gap will require further significant savings when the council is already struggling to deliver current-year savings.
